title: Philippine Airlines Returns to India With Nonstop Manila-Delhi and Mumbai Flights
excerpt: The Philippine flag carrier will fly nonstop from Manila to Delhi three times a week and Mumbai four times weekly from December 2026, pending Indian government approval — eight years after an earlier plan never took off.
body:
• Philippine Airlines will launch nonstop flights from Manila to Delhi and Mumbai in December 2026, subject to Indian government approval — three weekly flights to Delhi and four to Mumbai.
  • Both routes will use a 168-seat Airbus A321neo with 12 lie-flat Business Class seats and 156 Economy seats, departing Manila at 10:40 PM on each operating night.
  • PAL President Richard Nuttall called the routes a move to strengthen the airline's network "in one of Asia's most dynamic economies"; the carrier is also in the process of joining the oneworld alliance.
  • PAL had announced Delhi and Mumbai plans back in 2018 that never materialised; currently only Air India offers a direct Delhi–Manila flight.

A Direct Link Eight Years in the Making

Philippine Airlines is finally coming to India. The Philippine flag carrier announced on September 25 that it will launch nonstop services from Manila to Delhi and Mumbai starting December 2026, pending approval from the Indian government. Delhi gets three weekly flights (PR642 on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays) and Mumbai gets four (PR646 on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays).

The flights depart Manila at 10:40 PM, arriving in Delhi at 3:00 AM and Mumbai at 3:05 AM the following morning. Return legs leave Delhi at 8:15 AM and Mumbai at 7:15 AM, landing back in Manila by 5:00 PM.

"Opening services to Delhi and Mumbai strengthens PAL's network in one of Asia's most dynamic economies. These routes will create new opportunities for Filipinos to explore India while supporting the growing movement of travelers, businesses and goods between our two countries."

— Richard Nuttall, President, Philippine Airlines

Context & Background

This is not PAL's first attempt at India. The airline had announced Delhi and Mumbai services back in 2018, planning to use its new A321neo fleet — but those flights never took off. The market has changed considerably since. Air India currently operates the only direct flight between Delhi and Manila (with an A321neoLR since October 2025), while IndiGo has announced expansion involving Manila and Cebu.

PAL is also in the process of joining the oneworld alliance after receiving an invitation earlier in 2026, which makes the new routes considerably more relevant to frequent flyers in India — a market where oneworld membership is dominated by American Airlines, British Airways, Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines and Qantas.

Impact & Analysis

PAL is deploying a deliberately modest aircraft for the launch: a long-haul-configured Airbus A321neo with 168 seats, including a proper 12-seat lie-flat Business Class cabin. The narrowbody strategy mirrors Air India's own playbook on the Delhi–Manila corridor, letting the airline open the market without flooding it with capacity. The small premium cabin also means relatively few business seats per flight — potentially attractive for award redemptions once PAL's oneworld integration is complete.

The routes add cargo capacity between the two countries and, more importantly, give PAL a Manila hub connection story: travellers from Delhi and Mumbai can connect onward to Cebu, Boracay, Davao and other Philippine leisure destinations, or to PAL's international network spanning Los Angeles, Vancouver, Honolulu, Sydney, Brisbane, Perth, Melbourne, Tokyo Haneda and Hong Kong.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, this is a practical win rather than a symbolic one. The Philippines has quietly become a major destination for Indian travellers — Boracay and Cebu rank among Asia's most affordable beach holidays — but getting there from India has meant one-stop routings through Singapore, Bangkok or Hong Kong. A nonstop Delhi–Manila or Mumbai–Manila flight cuts that journey down sharply. There is also a meaningful connection: the Philippines hosts a sizable Indian community, concentrated in Manila's trading, textile and retail sectors, and these routes give that community its first direct link home. And for diaspora flyers holding oneworld status, a future PAL nonstop could become an interesting alternative for Australia and North America routings via Manila.

What's Next

The December launch is explicitly subject to Indian government approval, so schedules could shift. Watch for ticket sales opening in the coming weeks, fare positioning against Air India on the Delhi route, and any announcement on the Mumbai leg — PAL's first-ever service to the city. If approvals land as planned, December will bring another new airline and another nonstop option to the India–Southeast Asia market, just as IndiGo steps up its own Philippines plans.
nri_angle: Direct Manila flights give the Philippines' Indian community its first nonstop link to India, cut journey times for diaspora travellers to Boracay and Cebu, and add a future oneworld option for Australia and North America routings via Manila.
author: Diaspora Desk
